utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I first have to correct something for the record. When the Chamber decided to admit the two statements, that is one statement and the video-recorded interview, I had forgotten to add to that that the video is admitted as well, strictly not under 92 ter because 92 ter doesn't talk about videos, but it is, of course, so closely related to the -- to the transcript of the interview that it is admitted under the same exhibit number, which, therefore, comprises both video and transcript of the interview. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please do so. And I would like to remind you, Witness, Mr. Janic, that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. That is that you will speak the truth, whole truth and nothing but the truth. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wish to clarify, can I -- may I seek an extension of time for examination. I seek Court's indulgence. I had made a mistake in terms of estimating time and I would be grateful if I could be granted an extension of time, at least during the first session. I will try my best to finish within an hour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would try to finish within an hour. If it would be a little bit more than that, the Chamber would not immediately stop you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, can I call document 5222, please, 5222.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Janic, can you explain -- you can see the document, it is already up on the screen. This is an order issued by Mr. Markac dated 6 December 1999 to Lucko unit to send weapons for repairs and to be written off. Can you explain to us when weapons are written off, what happens to them? Are they destroyed or are they kept in some place?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain. Since at the moment I am the commander of a Special Unit in the MUP and I operate in the same manner, which is whenever a weapon is broken or is there is a suspicion that it's broken or if something turns up during regular annual checkups, there are two regular procedures as follows. The broken weapons, malfunctioning weapons are being repaired, if possible, and there is a commission in the MUP which deals with the writing off of these kind of weapons, and these are destroyed. These are not kept in storage. So that same procedure was applied then and it is still applied. So the weapons that is reparable is repaired. For instance, if it has a rusty or broken barrel this weapon is unusable and is written off, once a sufficient quantity is collected and it has to be done under the surveillance of a commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber doesn't have an English version of this document on its screen. Is there any explanation for that? So my B/C/S is still not good enough to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I was under the impression that there was an English copy uploaded to e-court. In fact, I looked at it last night.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is currently no English translation in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a hard copy somewhere nearby?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add something. All other services with the Ministry of Interior write off malfunctioning weapons. This does not apply only to the special police. This applies to the crime police and every other departments in the MUP. They carry out technical inspections, repairs, and the writing off of unusable weapons, and we are now part of that system, and we were part of that system before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, we can see the English translation on e-court on our system here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's not spend too much time on --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections. No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P578.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my understanding, Ms. Mahindaratne, this is to -- to give, to demonstrate how it works, the system, is that how?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have last night tendered other related documents and we will make the required submission later on to Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. Then, Mr. Registrar, you have said it was 578. P578 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document number 770, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Janic, permit me to take you to paragraph 65 of your statement, the 2004 statement. Now n paragraph 65, you say that you were in charge of a search operation that was in the area of Promina mountain on 26th August, 1995. And you described that operation. And then you say that the Lucko unit was also involved in that operation and Mr. Celic was in command of that operation, too, on the 26th. And you say: "I remember that almost as the operation began I was informed by a member of the Lucko unit that they had been in conflict with two enemy soldiers and that they had opened fire. I could hear explosions and shots fired." And at paragraph 66 you say: "After receiving this information I could see that something in a nearby village was on fire. I was also informed that the hand rocket launchers were used and as this village was near the railroad that the freedom train with President Tudjman and various diplomats was expected to travel and I contacted Mladen Markac who was in Knin at the time. I asked him to come and assist the situation himself. He arrived at the finish of the operation and I told him that there had been a conflict and that the two terrorists had got away. He asked how the houses -- "

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. "He asked how the houses caught fire and was not pleased that it had happened. He said that there would be an investigation into the burning of the houses. He was told by the Lucko unit that it was the use of the rocket launcher that caused the fire in the houses."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Janic, when you received that information from Mr. Celic that there was an incident, did you go into this village where the houses were on fire?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not immediately. I only went later.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And was that the Ramljane village. Perhaps I mispronounced that name. You know the village I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you visited later on how many houses had been burned? What did you observe?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few farming buildings were burned and perhaps one house. I didn't pass through the entire village. I just went as far as the entry to the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you said immediately when you received the information you called on Mr. Markac and Mr. Markac arrived there. Now, did Mr. Markac go to Ramljane village? You say that he was annoyed by the houses on fire. Did he go to the village and see the houses on fire? Or, I'm sorry, you said farm -- a few farming buildings and a house.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Markac came quite a bit later, so he didn't go into the village. All the information he had had about what happened there was received from me. I must say that I have made a striking mistake here. His driver told me that he was in Gracac but he was rather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters will kindly ask the speaker to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You really have to speak at a more moderate speed because the interpreters cannot follow you. If you would restart. You said Mr. Markac came quite a bit later so he didn't go into the village and all the information he had about what happened there was received from me. And then you said something about a mistake. Could you please resume there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that Mr. Markac was in Knin at the time. However he was in Gracac and that is why he was late, and couldn't make it in time. He only arrived after the action of that day was completed. The meeting that I convened at the end of the action with the people who took part in it and given that this armed clash had taken place, I felt the need, as the commander of the action, and since the train of freedom was due to arrive and this is the area very close to the railway track, I want the general to see for himself what it was all about because there was no doubt there was a conflict, a fighting, and that the burning was undoubtedly caused by the use of the hand-held rocket launchers. Therefore I had no doubts about the reports received from the commanders. However due to the delicate situation in the area I wanted him to become convinced about what I myself had become convinced. When I said that the general was not satisfied, of course he was not satisfied because this could have caused certain problems while the train of freedom were to pass through. At this meeting with the people who had taken part in the action, he expressed his dissatisfaction and said that he would conduct certain inquiries an investigations in order to establish whether actually what happened corresponds to what had been said and described. Later on, before departure, or before we went other own separate ways the general trusted me with verifying all this information and to interview the commander of the ATJ Lucko and other commanders in order to verify whether the reports were true. After these interviews, I established that this is exactly what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, if I could just -- it's been a while and let me, if I could, just take you to your interview notes. And that's the third section of P553, and I'm referring to transcripts 5309, page 43. And you say, you refer to the incident and I don't want to waste time reading all that. You say around line -- in the middle of -- around line 14: "And as I knew that General Markac was in the area at the time, just to make sure that there would be no problems because of the freedom train, I did not doubt in -- at any moment that the men had abused their power or abused the force or anything like that. I just called General Markac who was in the area and I knew that he could be there in some 20 minutes' time to go together and see what had happened just to make sure that there would be no problem for the freedom train the next day. And as my superior was in the area at the time, General Markac, I thought it would be prudent to call him." Then the question is asked: "Do you know where Mr. Markac was in the area at that particular time?" "No I do not know and I believe Mr. Markac subsequently came to the scene or to the area. Yes, of course, after I called him to come." Then you go on to say: I think the reason why he was in the area there was like a little stage set up where Tudjman took pictures with all the generals. You know he came out of the train. He went there. So Mr. Janic, I'm just trying to, perhaps if you have forgotten since it is a while, you indicated that at the time you heard Mr. Markac was there Zagreb from his driver. You said it in 2004 and now in 2005 that Mr. Markac was in the area and you called on him and when he came, you knew he could come within 20 minutes. Which of it is correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't understand me. I did not say now that he was Zagreb, but, rather that he was in Gracac. I had thought at the time that he was in Knin, and in that case he couldn't have made in 20 minutes. His driver told me that he been in Gracac. Therefore, he was not in Zagreb but in Gracac. This is a little bit wider area, but he was not in Knin; he was in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I made the mistake by saying Zagreb instead of Gracac.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that the freedom train and its main station was in Knin and all the generals, after the victorious operation received certain honours from the president, and all the lower-ranking officers who were directing the operation were there for the celebration. That was the reason for the arrival of all the generals involved in Operation Storm, to take part in the celebration.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, you go on to say at page 46 that -- you were asked the question: "Were you present when Mr. Markac addressed the members of the Lucko unit?" "Yes." So which member did Mr. Markac address in the Lucko unit? Was it the commander, Mr. Celic, who was a -- commanding the operation or any particular special instructor or any particular member? And --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a small unit, numbering between 30 and 35 men and he addressed all of them. But other members of other units were there as well. It was an area where the vehicles were, and all the people who had been involved in the action were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 50 you were asked this question: "Do you recall seeing Mr. Markac having a, like, almost face-to-face argument with Mr. Drljo?" Your response is: "I mean, I did, I did hear, you know, I can't say what was said between them. I mean, I could hear Drljo mumbling something but I was not close enough to hear what was said between them." And you're smiling, Mr. Janic, when I'm reading that. Did you recall that incident?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember in the same way as I described it in 2005. I saw them exchanging something, but I couldn't catch their words.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, was it a hostile exchange? Did it seem to you that the reason Mr. Markac was addressing Mr. Drljo in that fashion was because of the incident of the -- the buildings catching fire in Ramljane?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer because I didn't hear what they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Janic, any time after this incident, if Mr. Drljo or any member of the Lucko unit were investigated about that incident or if they -- if any disciplinary measures were meted out against any member of the Lucko unit?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, everything that happened on the 26th, I, as a commander, after conducting talks with platoon commanders and unit commanders established that there was no overstepping of authority and I did not treat it as any kind of incident. Therefore, there was no reason for imposing or launching any disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was a report submitted to you by Mr. Celic in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you -- when you visited the archives, Mr. Janic, did you see Mr. Celic's report on -- of the 26th?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did. I think I did. It was a written report, identical to an oral report, and based on his written report I compiled my own report, which was sent to the staff in Gracac as was the normal procedure, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now you say you sent your report to the staff in Gracac, as was the normal procedure. At paragraph 67 of your 2004 statement, Mr. Janic, if I could take you to it, that's P522. You say that you could not find your report on that operation when you checked the archives or any other report apart from one that General Markac submitted to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call up document number 1856, please. I'm sorry, Mr. President, I could not tender the previous document into evidence, which was 770, but I will get to that after -- I don't want to create confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, is this the document that you saw in the archives regarding this operation? This is Mr. Markac's report.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. Could you please pull it up a little so I can see the bottom of the page. Or perhaps I can move it myself, but I'm just not quite sure how.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we could go to the page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can you move to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the portion in relation to the Lucko ATJ, there was an armed clash that erupted and that is identical to my report, the report that I submitted. I see nothing about this that is questionable. This was a perfectly regular thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P579.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P579 is admitted into evidence. Apart from the previous document not being tendered or not being tendered yet, the relevance is not entirely clear to me at this moment. If you could please revisit that at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will call this up right now, Mr. President, while we're on this topic. Mr. Registrar, can I call back up document number 770.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, this is information sent by Mr. Markac to -- it says Split Military District and Knin forward command post, regarding activities which is to be carried out on 26th August 1995. Now, does this refer to the operation which was -- which we just spoke about, that is the operation in -- near the Promina mountains. That refers to the Ramljane village which we just discussed about.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And can you explain, do you know what the reference to the Knin IZM is?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't think I can help with you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just move this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit number P580, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. P580 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, just one question. Before every operation, was there an exchange of information such as this between the special police and the relevant HV commands in the area and any other authorities? Are you able to offer an answer to that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. We were the special police. We always planned our searches and our actions based on intelligence, based on intelligence gathered by the regular police, the districts, the district areas, the recruitment areas based on their requests based on any information that was available to them. It was important to go out, crush any groups of enemy soldiers. We needed to know where minefields were or any heavy weaponry that was left behind. We would then use this information and this information was pooled by internal control in the special police. They did intelligence analysis and they did security assessments. It was based on those security assessments by internal control that we planned our activities. So that is how the system worked. There was nothing random about any of our actions. We used those serious and thorough security assessments, we used all the intelligence that was available to us on certain security aspects that we covered all these areas and launched our actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document number 1050, please. And this is actually, Mr. President, a document I have submitted through the bar table motion, but it is on the face of it a little difficult to understand so I just require an explanation from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, can you just identify, I merely want you to identify if -- or confirm if in fact this is a report on the mop-up operation of 26th August 1995. And it's a handwritten very informal report, issued by the Krapina, and I beg your pardon for the mispronunciation, Zagorje Z-a-g-o-r-j-e, is that correct? Because we are unable to identify that on the face of this document, but you probably will be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please allow me to look at the bottom, or the end of this report, rather. Yes. That would be that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is one of the units that participated on 26th operation in the Promina mountain area?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to tender this document into evidence, and just for record keeping to indicate that this document has been included in the bar table motion last night so to -- there won't be duplicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, admitted into evidence, but, of course we first need a number. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P581.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P581 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document number 3506, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: While the document comes up, Mr. Janic, were you questioned about the Grubori incident by the Ministry of Interior police bureau in 2004, in the course of an investigation initiated by the county prosecutor of Sibenik in 2001. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who initiated that, but, yes, it was in 2004 that I was questioned by the crime police investigation. The office in which I was interviewed was actually just a stone's throw away from my own office in which I normally work. In answer to your question, yes, I was questioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in the course of that interview did they take down notes of your interview -- let me just -- to make it short. If you could look at the document in front of you and let us know if in fact it is an accurate note of your interview?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should probably read this in its entirety. But one thing I can tell you, I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, I didn't think so. That's why I would like to you take a look at it and tell us whether it is an accurate note.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please pull the document up a little? We can move on. And on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think we need to move to the next page. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And do you agree that it is an accurate note of your interview with the Ministry of Interior crime police, in 2004?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was interviewed and this note was drawn up, but the interview was not recorded, and no minutes were taken. So this is an interpretation of the interview that the police officer did following the interview. Therefore, it is not perfectly accurate. This was never submitted to me for approval or signature, this Official Note. In principle, the note changes nothing with respect to my previous and later statements but not all of the details are perfectly accurate and the context of some of this information is not exactly what I shared with the police officer during this interview at this time. I should assume that he drew this up based on his memory of our interview and that might be the reason that it is not perfectly accurate. The other thing I wish to say is this. I'm still with the police. Therefore, I can say this: Official Notes such as this one cannot be used in court proceedings. This is not admitted into evidence, a document like this, in our own system and Official Notes such as these cannot be used as exhibits. It is just one thing I wanted to say. I'm not sure how you deal with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're looking at me, Mr. Janic. This Tribunal is not bound by any domestic system as far as the law of evidence is concerned and how we're going to deal with it. I appreciate your interest in criminal procedure. At the same time, if you would focus on the questions, that would also be appreciated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would have an objection on this, Your Honour. What is the basis for this document be taken into the evidence because this is not the statement of the witness which is sitting here in front of us. This is an note made by the police officer in Zagreb police administration. So I think the proper basis would be to discuss this document with the police officer who is the author of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has confirmed that this is a note based on an interview between himself and a police officer and with regard to the inaccuracies, the Defence has the -- can explore the inaccuracies in the course of cross-examination. I have established a basis for the admission of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I know, I rise to my feet just because of the general nature and the impact this would have on other statements, but I would note that the Office of the Prosecutor has witness statements that it has taken by its investigators which we've attempted to tender which have been denied admission, so I'm not sure if the witness has not made the 92 ter attestations pursuant to Rule 92 ter that this is a statement of his and I'm not sure what the difference is between a statement taken by a police officer in Croatia and then a statement taken by an OTP investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the difference is that if a statement is taken by an OTP investigator that the statement is taken for the purpose of investigations and prosecution before this Tribunal. If you would like at the case law, then you will see that sometimes contemporaneous or at least all the statements that not taken for the purposes of one of the parties in the trials before this Tribunal are dealt with in a different way than statements taken specifically to serve as -- as evidence in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I may just follow up with that, Your Honour, for future guidance. If statements are taken by the Croatian police or Croatian prosecutors pursuant to their criminal cases or notes, I should say, those statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you look -- if you compare for example, and that is one of the examples that comes immediately into my mind, in the Haradinaj case quite a lot of statements were taken from suspects and witnesses at the time approximately when the events had happened, not for the purpose of being used in this Tribunal but for different purposes, those were admitted into evidence, not under Rule 92 ter, and of course the Chamber will consider, I mean we're not in a hurry with it at this moment, but at least there is an -- a difference. Another matter is what weight to give, whether the Chamber would accept the statement as -- as solid evidence for the truth of its content. That is of course a different matter. At least this document, so apart from the decision of the Chamber will be, demonstrates also in connection with the testimony of this witness that there was an interview. Apparently there was an investigation and that at least a report was made of that interview. I mean, to that extent the statement would have some probative value, not necessarily about what happened in 1995 but at least what happened later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand Your Honour and I don't want to take more time I just wish to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is not a decision but I just wanted to point out the difference between statements taken for the specific purpose of being used as evidence before this Tribunal and statements taken in a different context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just one minor point, Your Honour, and I understand the reasoning there. However, I will look and see if there is any case law on this, but statements taken for these proceedings by the opposing party to me would tend to be a different situation than for example a Gotovina defense witness statement and then us tendering it. But let's have that discussion I guess for a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But I understand the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know who's opposing party to whom in this context, but we'll consider it. And, Mr. Tieger, perhaps it is good if we have Mr. Mikulicic to say first. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I will just add one little remark on it. This is anonymous note. We don't know who the author is. There is no sign, there is no name on it. We don't know how could we check on the note whether this is accurate or no. This is just a remark as it relates to the credibility of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we usually do is under those circumstances is to seek further information from the party presenting the evidence to explain where it originates from and then of course with that knowledge we can further consider whether that is sufficient information, whether it is accepted by the Defence or whether that needs further exploration. Mr. Tieger, you were on were your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just quickly, Your Honour, because Mr. Misetic rose on a matter of a general nature and I just wanted to make sure that a specific instance wasn't expanded into and across the board principle of any type. So with reference to previous attempted submissions made by Mr. Misetic, I don't recall, in fact, a precisely analogous situation where a statement made by the particular witness on the stand was presented to him. So I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have some difficulties there identifying what Mr. Misetic was exactly referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So it is not necessarily simply the nature of the document that is only relevant issue in determining admissibility at any point; it's also the context. And that is all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My point is that he is on the stand and because he is on the stand we have rules under Rule 92 ter on how those statement would say be admitted which is why I then drew the broader analogy concerning the reliability of whatever statements are taken outside the context of a specific case. Clearly 92 ter has not been met here so we're obviously applying a different set of rules, and then I was just saying that if we could define a little bit which statements get in and which statements don't. My general point was that I don't see in terms of the probative value much difference between a statement taken by the Croatian police and a statement taken by the Prosecution but tendered by the Defence, but, like I said, this is more of a general topic and perhaps we can have it at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As matters stand now we'll invite Mr. Registrar to mark this document for identification. Ms. Mahindaratne, you have heard that Mr. Mikulicic has some difficulties with the origin of this document. If there's anything that could be submitted in that respect the Chamber will hear from you. And, Mr. Registrar, this will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would be exhibit number P582 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that will be the status for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, and we will submit evidence in due course of it's -- regarding the authenticity -- the origin, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Before you just move on to the next topic while we're still on your statement, Mr. Janic, if I could take you to paragraph 70 of your statement, 2004. You refer to check-points there. And you say that: "After 8th August 1995, when the main Operation Storm was over, there were fundamental police check-points but we were not stopped as we were on official business and would not really have the authority to stop us. I do not recall any military check-points, although there were military police check-points, but they had no authority to stop us. The military police check-points s were apart from the fundamental police check-points. These check-points usually consisted of a car or two parked by the side of the road. The purpose of these check-points was for the fundamental police to check civilians' identification and to check if they had any weapons or any looted items. And the military police check-point was to check military personnel." Now my question was if the fundamental police did not have authority to stop the special police, who had the authority to stop the special police if members of the special police were observed committing crimes? And I'm not suggesting to you now to contemplate on whether they committed crimes or not. My question is who would have the authority to stop them if they were observed committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you look at paragraph 70, this is where I offer my somewhat liberal interpretation. Of course something happens, someone stops someone else at any sort of check-point, regular or special police, even special policemen would have to stop. But as a rule they didn't stop us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, please, I'm running out of time. If could you just answer as to who, which force had the authority to stop special police and perhaps arrest them if they were observed committing crimes. That's my question to you, and if could you try to answer that as briefly as possible.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about this specific case. I didn't understand you to be asking me a general question. If there is a special police member who commits a crime all the general regulations are applied as to all other citizens and then it is the regular police that would have the authority to arrest them. The procedure would probably be to inform his superior commander and then his superior commander would help and the local police would help arrest that person. It would be the local police station that would have the responsibility under the law to arrest this person who possibly committed a crime in the line of duty. That's what the law says, as long as a crime was committed, of course. What I was talking about is being pulled over while driving down a road at some check-point or other, that is what I was referring to. But if there is a crime that occurs that the same laws apply to special police members as they do to any other citizen, and the regular police has the responsibility to take the same kind of action or the same kind of steps with respect to anyone. In paragraph 70 what I was referring to was traffic checks. They would never stop us. We were in special police vehicles and they were the regular police. You hardly ever see police stopping another police vehicle. It wasn't done back then and I don't think it is even done nowadays in 2008. It is an extremely rare occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you ever see -- you say that the military police check-points was to check military personnel. Did you see military personnel being checked at military check-points or being stopped at military check-points?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, following the 8th or the 9th of August, the army was no longer deployed in those areas and wasn't moving in those areas. They were either in barracks or moving towards the Bosnia-Herzegovina border. As of that date, I did not see any of the Croatian army units moving along that area. The MPs were there, but I personally never saw them stop anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document number 1665, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, while the document comes up I draw your attention to paragraph 33 of your 2004 statement where you refer to the liberation of Gracac. Now, this is a report going from Mr. Markac to the chief of Croatian army Main Staff, General Cervenko. Is this an accurate report, because you were commanding this line of special police that liberated Gracac?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is not quite true what you suggest. I was the commander of one of the axes during that operation. I was responsible for some segments of the special police. The report, however, is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit number P583, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P583 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 47 -- I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar, may I call document number 1664, please. Now, Mr. Janic, in paragraph 47 you refer to setting up the special police headquarters in Gracac once it was liberated. Now, before I ask you the question, could you just take a look at this document and tell us if this is an accurate report? It reports that on 5th August 1995 by 1130 hours the special police units took complete control over Gracac, and by 1200 hours they have taken control of the Celavac and Prezid areas. Is that a correct -- accurate report?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P584.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P584 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, once the special police headquarters was set up in Gracac on 5th August, till when did the special police operate from Gracac from that headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember now exactly. There are some documents bearing some date. I saw these dates. I think it was in October or November, but I cannot be sure. After perusing through the documents before my arrival here, I remember seeing the exact date but cannot remember it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In paragraph 75, you say that you saw -- I'll read it just the way it is recorded: "As far as General Markac was concerned I would see him fairly regularly, both during and after the operation. I would see Mr. Sacic as often as I would see General Markac." Now, did you see Mr. Markac and Mr. Sacic at the headquarters in Gracac? Where did you see them regularly?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the headquarters in Gracac. Of course they were not there everyday but they were often there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move to -- I don't know whether document has been given a number. I move to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, isn't this the same document as was assigned number P584?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then it has been admitted into evidence already.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 25, line 23. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I missed that. Mr. Registrar, may I call Exhibit number P325, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, in paragraph 28, you describe the special police uniforms and you say: "Our uniform at the time during the whole of Operation Storm was light green plain uniform with green helmets. I believe that we wore yellow ribbons on our shoulders during the operation for identification purposes." Can you identify the photograph -- the people in these pictures, are they members of the special police? Based on the uniform can you say that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could move to perhaps the next photograph, I think it is a more clearer picture, if Mr. Janic wants to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You can see the insignia clearer on this picture.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Judging by the insignia on their uniforms, these are the insignia of military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You said military police. Did you refer to special police. Was it --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I said special police. It may have been mistranslated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And there was evidence led and this in fact to the effect that the units or commander of this unit identified the unit as the Delta unit and this was on 8th August in Gracac. Do you know, in fact, if the Delta unit was in Gracac on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was, but I would have to look it up in the documents. I think that in Gracac on the 5th of August, as far as I can remember, a group from this unit ran into a Serbian ambush and one of the members of the unit was killed. That was immediately after they entered the town. While they were entering the town there was no fighting going on, because the Serbian forces had actually fled. However, there were some Serbian forces that were staying behind on a truck and they opened fire from their truck and that is how one of our members was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could I ask one further question on the colour of the ribbons. Please correct me when I'm wrong, but it's my recollection that in one of the previous documents we saw in which there was planning of an operation, I think it was for the 26th of August, that other colours of ribbons or arm-bands were used for identification purposes. Is my recollection correct, which would mean that not only yellow ribbons but other circumstances, other arm-bands or ribbons or whatever of a different colour would be used in order to identify the special police forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain that to you. We used yellow ribbons during Operation Storm but we as a unit also had other coloured ribbons in our storage house for other operations. I suppose that these ribbons cannot last for 20 days. These yellow ribbons were used specifically for Operation Storm. Before that, there was Operation Flash when I think red ribbons were used, so these changes were introduced for tactical reasons. At one point one type of ribbons were replaced by another ribbons in a different colour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could assist, I think your reference was to a document which gave information about a mop-up operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes it is. My problem is that if once it is upload so that we can see it, it takes a while before we can have access to it, if it is admitted into evidence. But I think that that was the planning letter dated 25th of August for the operations on the 26th, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If anyone would have the exhibit number then we could put it on the record just for the convenience of those who would later consult this transcript. But, otherwise, please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's P579, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, it is P580, not 579.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then thank you for that number as well, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now one other question on this, Mr. Janic. I don't have much time. Do you remember what colour ribbons were worn by the special police units in the course of the operation in Plavno on 25th August?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document number 2760, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, while the document comes up, I refer you to paragraph 34 of your statement where you describe the liberation of Donji Lapac. Is this -- this is a report going from Mr. Markac to General Cervenko regarding the capture of Donji Lapac. Is this an accurate report?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we have it scrolled up a bit, please. Can I see the end, please. Roughly speaking, it would be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move to tendere this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P585.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P585 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, drawing you to paragraph 37 of your statement you say: "When I entered Donji Lapac I saw about -- " further down. I don't want to waste time reading the entire paragraph. You say: "When we entered the town it was being shelled but by the afternoon the shelling had stopped." In paragraph 36 you say: "When I reached Donji Lapac, some of the buildings were burning in the centre, including the police station. I heard that was done by the artillery fire. I did not go through the whole town but what I saw was not too badly damaged." Now, in relation to that, let me take to you what you have said at the interview, and that would be P553, the second set. That is 5308, page 11. There you're referring to the liberation of Donji Lapac. You say -- and you were asked the question: "And did you use again -- did you again use artillery support?" This is in relation to Donji Lapac. You say: "No. There was no need because there was no resistance, there was no conflict. We did not encounter anybody so there was no need." Again, you go on to express, you say: "There was no need for a sort of prior artillery fire that would come before us because the situation was such that the enemy was running away. They were -- the atmosphere was such that basically we felt that we didn't need any prior artillery before we moved." And then there is an discussion as to what other people have said about this. Then you -- in paragraph 13, line 14 you say: "Truly, there was no need for it and that is why I did not use this possibility." Now, can you then explain as to now you as the commander of that particular axis of attack did not consider artillery support necessary for that. Do you know why it was used, why in fact the town was shelled?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave my statement from the position of the role that I had at the time, which is a commander of the main axis. On my axis there was no resistance and no fighting and I did not use artillery support because I did not need it. I don't know about the other axis. I know that the army of the district of Gospic covering the whole of Lapac was there, but I don't know if they used artillery or not. My report refers only to my line of attack and my zone, in which I personally did not use any artillery support for either in-depth targets or any strongholds directly facing my forces. There was no need for that because everybody had fled. However, whether at the beginning of the operation they were in the area of Lapac around the town, I cannot say. I am talking about the situation in which I was and I'm talking about this from my own position. I cannot tell anything about other axes from the special police nor about what the army did with regard to the use of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And your axis went through the town of Donji Lapac, went through Donji Lapac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. My axis was called the main one. However, it stretched somehow along the shortcut but it also traversed the highest hills, and the final objective was to reach the roads around Donji Lapac and the town itself. Therefore, we were the last to reach the town, and there was no fighting for the town, so we virtually walked into it. There was no fighting either in the town or around town at the time when I arrived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us at what time you did arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure. Around 12.00 or 1.00. Maybe one can find this information in the reports. But I think it was around 1.00 or 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document number -- I'm sorry, can I tender this document into evidence. I don't know if that was done. I may have missed out. There was -- the document that was on the screen, that was?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, this was admitted as P585.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call document number 5011, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, while that document comes up Mr. Janic, in paragraph 38 of your statement, you refer to military units arriving in Donji Lapac in the afternoon of 7th August. And if you could look at this document that's on the screen that refers to what happened in Donji Lapac, and, in fact, your involvement in addressing the matter with the unit commanders of the military, units that arrived Donji Lapac. Mr. Janic, you're looking at another document. Could you just look at the screen. Is this an accurate report? This refers to you addressing unit commander of the military about burning and problems in Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is accurate, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you ever find out why the military units were setting fire to houses in Donji Lapac? Did the unit commanders tell you what was going on?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since special police forces, at the time when they entered the town, were immediately deployed out of town, which means that there were no special police in the town with the exception of our specialist logistical base from which we were supplied with food and other stuff. On the late afternoon of the 7th when the army from the district -- military district of Gospic arrived --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, if I could just interrupt, my question was, did you -- and please try to confine your response to my question. Did you find out from the military unit commanders with whom you spoke as to why the units kept burning houses through the night? What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not find out about that. I was at this meeting. I warned the officer there about the situation, and as much as I could do in my position, I requested this to stop. So that was my entire exchange that I had with him. I considered that my warning would be sufficient for them to move and restore order in their units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And at your debriefing with Mr. Markac on 9th August, did you inform of this, the burning of the houses in Donji Lapac by military units, according to this report?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when, but I did inform him. I told him about my meeting with the military and that I requested them to restore order within their forces. However, on what date it was, I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P586.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P586 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call up document number 3342, please. And this is my last couple of questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did. I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is an order from Mr. Markac addressed to all special police unit chiefs and there are a couple of units excepted and then the head of special police sector anti-terrorist unit commander, that Lucko anti-terrorist commander and the airborne unit commander. And if you could scroll down to paragraph 2 of the English version, amongst the many orders he orders the units, in this way: "Unit commanders and department heads with the special police sector shall forthwith take measures to ensure civilised professional and lawful execution of official assignments of the special police members, thus eliminating arrogance and haughtiness in dealing with the population." Now, this document is dated 15th November. What was the basis for this order? It presupposes that there was some observed irregularities during the operation which is referred and that there was uncivilised and unlawful conduct because it clearly orders not to do that. What was the basis for this order?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I just cannot see whether this order is related to the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That might transpire or not transpire from the answer to this question. That is still to be seen. Ms. Mahindaratne is certainly not asking to you speculate. Do you know what the basis is for this order where apparently measures are taken to avoid in the future certain kind of misconduct? Do you know what triggered or what events triggered this order to be issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you an accurate answer. I was head of the department at the time and it applied to all my men. I know that there were lots of problems where the special forces returned from the field and they acted sort of arrogantly within their local community and there was some conflicts with those who were not involved in war. For instance, if a person went back to Pula, the special police -- military police were proud and treated somewhat arrogantly other people who did not take part in the war. This happened in cafes and in their free time. I don't know what prompted the general to issue this order, but I think that what he wanted to see better discipline in that part because there was no lack of discipline while they were on duty. It happened most of the time off duty. And under the law, they are obliged to behave themselves according to the law, whether they're on duty or off duty. I think this is the -- the point of this particular paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I move this document into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P587.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P587 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to wait for the witness to answer that question, but I just want to point out that interruption in the presence of the witness was inappropriate giving the material to witnesses. I hope Defence counsel will not repeat that conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From my answer to your objection, Mr. Mikulicic, you may have noted that I thought that it would have been wiser to wait for the answer, and if that is wiser, then is preferred to refrain from intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not dramatic at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That concludes examination-in-chief. Mr. President, I apologise for the time I took beyond the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then have a break first. We'll then have a break and resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness, Mr. Janic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac and he will now cross-examine you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Janic. I will asking you questions on behalf of Mr. Markac's Defence. Please answer to the best of your knowledge and recollection. I would also like to ask you the following. Try to give our interpreters a decent chance to do their work while answering your questions. May I also ask you to pause between our questions and our answers, since we both speak the same language. Mr. Janic, you are a long-time police officer and you are fully trained. How long have you been working with the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been a member of the special police for over 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You went to certain schools during your career with the special police. Can you tell us briefly what sort of training you underwent?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean background as in education or do you mean other kinds of training?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I mean both, actually.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to secondary police school, the higher police school and the police academy. I have a degree in criminology. I underwent various types of specialist training, mostly to do with anti-terrorism; for example, hostage stage situations, planes getting kidnapped mountaineering, parachuting, crisis management. I was in charge of some of these training sessions and courses myself and I attended some of these, and there has been a lot of that going on over my career with the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this answer. Obviously we would be justified in assuming that you are something of an exceptional case within the special police. But can you tell us what sort of training special police officers normally get.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Special police officers are, nevertheless, police officers. Therefore, they undergo usual police training. They have to know about Croatia' laws and the laws as relate to the police, the Law on Criminal procedure, the Criminal Code and all general laws and regulations. They have to be familiar with all these rules that the work of each and every police officer is subject to. They have to know the rules of procedure. The fact is we're talking about special police. Therefore, there is also additional specialist training, which normally comprises a large number of specialities. This was first done in the 1990s when the special police units were first set up and this practice has continued into this very day, 2008. Special police officers study anti-terrorist tactics which teaches them what to do in certain situations, planes being kidnapped, ships being kidnapped, dealing with hostage situations and how to get hostages released and various types of situations. I could go on like that because is there more.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this is an typo here, page 38, line 15. Special police is noted down as military police. I just wanted -- it is a small point, but I just wanted to point that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Janic, would you agree with me that the principle purpose of the special police, since it is a component of Croatia's police, generally speaking, would be to restore law and order whenever law and order are under any significant threats?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When the war in Croatia first began and when the need arose for special police units to be involved in certain types of military activity, did the special police units not have to undergo some form of military training?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was most certainly the case. Throughout the early 1990s large tracts of Croatia's territory were under occupation. Each citizen had a commitment to Croatia. They had to take up weapons and defend their country and the same applied to the police. The special police was an elite branch of Croatia's police so obviously we work under an obligation to join in. We had specialist knowledge and special skills and the expectations were great in that respect. Special police officers underwent both specialist training, regular police training and military training, in addition to that. We were involved in war operations between 1990 and 1995. The training included tactical training of all members, in the sense of infantry tactics, and also artillery training. We were trained how to clear mines, how to use anti-tank or anti-armour weapons. We were taught to deal with intelligence, gather intelligence, and use intelligence that we received. This was also part of our specialist training and there was a part of our training that was meant to familiarize with all sorts of international conventions and laws. So that, too, was part of our training.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Let's try and say a thing or two about the makeup of the special police units and I'm talking primarily about their ethnic makeup. What about the standards or requirements that were required for someone to become a member of the special police unit? Did this ever follow ethnic, religious or other lines of that nature or were there other criteria applied?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none of those were applied. Then, as now, was only standard that applied was skill and ability on the part of an individual candidate both in mental and purely physical terms, so those were the requirements that needed meeting. As long as someone met all those requirements they would be in a position to become members of the special police but this was never done along ethnic or religious lines. I never heard of anything like that happening and I was there all the time. I knew exactly what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you for example confirm this for me, Mr. Skender Hasimi [phoen], an ethnic Albanian was a special police commander in the Pula police administration. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Ile Taletovic, a Muslim. He held the same post in the Dubrovnik police administration. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Hamdija Masinovic, another Muslim who was a commander with the Bjelovar police administration?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this a matter in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear it, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Could we please have a 65 ter document, 5031. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, a document is about to come up on your screen. It shows the structure of the special police units of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in slightly to allow the witness to see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us try to remind ourselves of how the structure worked, how the system worked. Please have a look first and then tell me if you think the chart faithfully reflects what you know about the system and how it worked.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a chart of the special police sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the chief of sector is the boss in a manner of speaking, right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All right. In the left-hand side of our screens we see a box that says internal control sector. This will come up again during our evidence here but we see that there is someone who is the head of this unit and they have internal control inspectors, as they call them. Now, in what way exactly was this sector a part of particular units of the special police? Can you tell me anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't directly work with this sector, but they had their own man in each of the units and then they would receive reports from each of the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, request the English translation would be provided later on by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. It just came on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is a 65 ter document and I believe there is translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It just came on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct me if I'm wrong, sir, of course the images you're looking at are somewhat smaller now and that makes it more difficult for you to see. Within this sector we have the terrorism prevention department, then we have the Lucko anti-terrorist unit, the air force unit, the psychological and propaganda department, and the last thing we see is the logistics department. That tallies with what you know about how this worked, right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we please move on to the next page of this document. 06119428. What we're looking is another chart. This is the internal structure of the special police units and they are attached to various police administrations of the Ministry of Interior. You've already mentioned that in each of the police administrations across the country there was a special police unit attached to it headed by a commander. Now, a special police unit commander, who did he answer to within the structure of the police administration?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All right. So this commander had an assistant commander and then we see who else worked within this same framework. If we move on to the next page --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the registrar to help us with this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We see a list and a job description for each of these units, for each of these units that were part of the overall composition. There is one thing that I would like to dwell on briefly. 06119434, this shows us the composition, the structure of the anti-terrorist unit, the specialist anti-terrorist unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So if we could go to the last page of this document. Okay. This -- that's the one, that's the one. Thank you. I'm always referring to the number in the upper right-hand corner. Maybe if there is any other way to proceed with this, I would be glad to be instructed on it. Okay, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we see here is a job description for the anti-terrorist unit. You mentioned earlier on, Mr. Janic, that in some way the anti-terrorist unit was an elite unit in practical terms. Can you please briefly explain what led you to you reach that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the other units were special units. The Lucko ATJ was an anti-terrorist unit and the requirements that this unit had to face were higher, in terms of mental criteria, in terms of physical ability, the requirements were greater. The bar was set higher. And its area of activity covered Croatia's territory in its entirety. This was more like a unit that was active throughout Croatia's territory and it didn't have so much to do with local police administrations and I think the same situation applies now. For example they control the air space and whenever something happens there, there is only one unit in the country that can deal with the situation. For example, if have you have a very complex hostage situation and this may or not may not occur. This is the only unit that could deal with it, there are a number of other peculiarities that are attached to the work of this unit but this would be it for our present purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned certain peculiarities. Do you think that includes a particularly high level training when it came to clearing mines, dealing with explosives and such-like?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was most certainly the case. The Lucko ATJ then, as now, had all the best trained people to deal with mines and explosives, especially explosives placed under water. For example, clearing torpedos and anti-naval mines and explosives. There is no other unit in Croatia that can actually deal with situations of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. We're looking at this document but this document as a matter of fact contains a number of documents. It is made up of a number of documents and we see there a part which actually comes from the decree on the internal structure and the principles of work of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia and this is a decree passed on the 23rd February 1995 by Croatia's government. We can move on to the next page and this is 06119435. As soon as we're there, we can look at the bottom of the page and you see there is talk there of the special police sector. This is page 12 of the pertinent document. And then we move on to the next page and we see paragraph 28.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Mikulicic referred to decree, but I could not follow from which page you were citing, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The whole decree as -- I mean in total, is under the ID number 3D00-1502 but this particular part of that decree which I'm referring on is part of the 65 ter that I mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'll try to catch up later on, Mr. President. I'm sure we will make the connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sure there will be no dispute on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about paragraph 28. Paragraph 28 talks about internal control within the special police sector. This is what the law says: "Internal control department undertakes measures and activities aimed at collecting, processing and using intelligence related to internal discipline within the special police, terror groups and their activities as well as other activities posing a serious threat to human lives and property." The department also works on security protection of the special police, equipment, weapons as well as any other tasks in which special police members are involved. It goes on to say that this department works with the service for the protection the constitutional order, they work on refining security-related information, intelligence, and this is something that is used for carrying out tasks peculiar to the work of the special police units and the department has a head who is in charge of this department. Mr. Janic, you say that each unit had its own -- in each unit there was a representative or a man belonging to the internal control department. Based on your memory we're talking about 1995, the same time as Operation Storm, were these the tasks and responsibilities that these representatives of theirs would be carrying out across the units?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The department itself and these men from that department had one principal task: Collecting intelligence, analysing intelligence, exchanging intelligence, and then there was the intelligence service of the Croatian army and the service for the protection of the constitutional order and there were a number of other service services that worked in gathering intelligence in order to pool all this intelligence from all of these various branches and services and then what they did was they drew up security assessments that had to do with certain areas and activities carried out by the special police. You might call this the intelligence department, just that it simply couldn't be called that and therefore it was called internal control. It wasn't possible to call it intelligence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
