utterances.text: Mr. Janic, do you know that the sector for internal control conducted any disciplinary procedures or did it instigate or process disciplinary measures against members of the police?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not within their jurisdiction concerning the internal order within the Ministry of Interior, and I may say that the same situation prevails today. Disciplinary proceedings were instigated by unit commanders or superiors. If you have a police station and a policeman from that station commits a misdemeanour, then the head or the chief of the police station will launch disciplinary proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is an request to slow down. That means both speed of speech but also a pause between questions and answer and answer and question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm, okay. [Interpretation] Similarly, according to the same principle the person authorised to instigate disciplinary proceedings within the special police was the commander of a specific unit, so one of his responsibilities was to institute disciplinary proceedings for disciplinary breaches within his units. If I were to commit one, then the disciplinary proceedings against me would have had to be instigated by the head of the sector. However, the internal control sector did not have within its purview any competence or authority to institute disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have this document admitted into evidence and that a number be assigned to it as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number D526.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D526 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can have now document 3D00-1502, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What we are about to see on our screens, Mr. Janic, is a decree issued by the government of the republic of Croatia setting up the internal structure and the modus operandi of the Ministry of Interior. For the sake of me asking you a question, only one section of this decree has been translated and I'm going to refer it now. Article 2 of this decree specifies the structure of certain parts within the ministry. It mentions the office, the chief of office, the sectors, sections et cetera. However, we are going to dwell on Article 4, and if we can look at the next page of this decree, please. This article stipulates the structure of the unit which is called the cabinet or the office of the minister. We're not going to go into the specific responsibilities of this office. However, I would like to draw your attention to Article 8, which speaks about the office of internal control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we please see Article 8. That's two pages ahead in the Croatian document. And can we please have the upper part of the page enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Article 8 stipulates that within the office of the minister an office for internal control will be set up. So this unit is called here office, unlike the unit within special police units where it is called a section. Let us look at what this article says. By operating with all sectors of the ministry, the internal control office should systematically gather data and report which indicate various forms of illegal conduct by officials and so on and so forth. Are you familiar with how this office operated, which was attached to the office of minister, and which has a similar name to the one that we discussed before?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This office exists today and it is also part of the office of the minister. Its jurisdiction today is the same as it is written here, which means that it independently gathers information and reports about any illegal or unlawful conduct by members of the police. It conducts checks in the field and then decides how to act on this information. Therefore, it is not part of the police structure in terms that it is above the police but, however, it is independent and is allowed to independently investigate the conduct of police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This office for internal control set up within the office of the minister, in a position of kind of subordinations or second-instance organ within the special police relating to internal control?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office for internal control of the office of the minister is completely independent in its work. The internal control department of the special police must provide certain information if the office asks for it and it is their duty to provide this information, just like any other department within the Ministry of the Interior and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a number assigned to this document. Then I would like to tender into evidence this section that has been translated.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number D527.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D527 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we look now at document 65 ter 02452, we'll see that this document, which will soon appear on our screens, is an annual report of the special police sector. If we move to the next page, we can see that this document was issued on the 22nd February 1996, that it was addressed to the minister of the interior, Mr. Jarnjak, and that this is a report relating to the year 1995. What I'm interested in in this document is that this is a report covering also the work of the internal control section, and that is on page 8 in the Croatian version. While we're waiting -- that's page 8. Bottom part, if we can have it enlarged, please. It says here that the internal control section of the special police took part in operational and intelligence preparations of all operations and actions in which members of the special police were participating. Accordingly, it says that good cooperation was in place with intelligence administration of the Main Staff of the Croatian army and the service for the protection of the internal order. The cooperation with MUP in terms of equipment was also good in terms of establishing monitoring centres and things like that. Then it says that there was exchange of information with other services with a view to gaining an insight into the overall situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just point out for the record so that there won't a confusion later on, this is one of the documents that was submitted through the bar table submission last night so there would not be any duplicity in marking exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I may take it that at least there will be no objection on behalf of the Markac Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: There will be no objection, Your Honour, that's for sure but it's quite hard to, you know, follow up this exchange of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one blames you for not having seen that, if it is true what Ms. Mahindaratne says. I have not checked that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to this report. I suppose you would agree with the content of this report, as far as internal control section was concerned. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. I fully agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this document admitted, but before we move on, I suppose that my learned colleague had also admitted the remaining parts of this report, which are numerical data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So let us take a look at the part of the document which contains numerical data that is on page 03549942. This is a table depicting the makeup of the special police in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be on the next page, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, what we see here is a list of special police units that were attached to various police administrations. The last one we see will is the Lucko ATJ. The first column shows us the internal structure numbers. The second column gives us figures in relation to 1995. It tells about the respective strengths of all these units back in 1995. The next thing that we can see is the ethnic makeup of each of the special police units. If we look at this we see that the internal makeup of the Lucko ATJ went like this: 190 members strength at the moment 75 per cent. What does this mean strength at the moment, since this is a report about 1995? Well, I just best allow to you explain this.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that in terms of its internal makeup the unit could have a maximum of 190 members. We're talking about the Lucko ATJ now. But at this point in time it only had 75 actual employees in the unit, police officers. Operation Storm had been concluded and then Operation Flash before so many people were killed and wounded and this affected the makeup of the unit and other units as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection how many members of the Lucko ATJ were there in August and September 1995? I'm talking about the time when the search operations were conducted.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there were over 50 of them. Later on during the searchs, maybe about 40 members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next page talks about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... would you mind if I put a question in relation to the page which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me check whether that is on our screen. Yes. You earlier explained to us that the composition of the special police forces was not determined by anything else than skill and -- nevertheless, it appears from this table that it was an almost mono-ethnic force. Do you -- is that -- do you have an explanation why more than 98 of the force consists of Croats where apparently in recruiting, the ethnicity or the nationality didn't play a role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have an explanation, as a matter of fact. Special police units are not mobilised. One volunteers to become a member. There are a certain number of volunteer but they must meet certain requirements to become members. Therefore, one reports as a volunteer in order to join a unit like this. If no persons of other ethnicities within Croatia reported or volunteered, then there was no one to admit into the special police. So this was the only requirement that was applied. One must submit a written application expressing one's desire to undergo certain tests to see if this person was fit to join one of the special police units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what kind of tests were these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Various kinds of tests. Stamina, durability, running, speed of reaction, marksmanship, martial arts, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you were earlier asked whether the ethnic background or the national background of the members played any role, of course I would have expected you to answer that question by saying no, it didn't play a role at all, but we had hardly any applicants from other-than-Croatian background, or those applicants of non-Croatian background didn't pass the tests. I don't know what the case was, but that would have been a complete answer to the question, Mr. Janic. Of course now we see the numbers and I put this question to you, but that would put a better assist to the Chamber that answer than just saying no ethnic or nationalist background didn't play any role. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Could we please move on to page 03549946, same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is an overview of forms of training for special police members throughout 1995, the various kinds of training that were implemented through 1995. While introducing this subject you told us about the training and education of the special police members and this was a very important segment of their work. I'm looking at this document and I'd like to move on to the last page of this document. This is 948. I'm talking about the last three digits. The last page reads -- right. Throughout 1995 20 courses were organised and held, attended by 1134 members of the special police. There were a total of 16 seminars attended by 533 members or employees. Throughout 1995 there were various forms of specialist training. 1667 members of the special police underwent this and about 100 members of the Ministry of Interior special police units from the neighbouring republic of Herceg-Bosna following approval by the minister. They all took these courses that were organised, and the seminars. Mr. Janic, is that in keeping with your own recollection about these courses that were organised and held and about attendance, the attendance figures specifically?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This tallies with what I know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Needless to say, whenever you have something that you feel you need to explain and when you feel that a simple answer would not remain unambiguous, please provide any explanations that you might feel are necessary?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For example, about 60 per cent of these seminars and courses were run by my own department, organised by my own department. Therefore I was directly in contact with this type of work. I was myself in charge of some of these seminars. I offered certain lectures, for example, and I was involved in organizing these courses. This was part of our work and whenever our men were not busy conducting operations elsewhere we would work on training by organising courses and seminars such as these.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now please move on to page 953, same document. This is a table training level for special police leaders, and you may have said a thing or two about this already. If we look at this table we can see the training levels for each of the ranks, department chief, inspectors, commanders, assistant commanders and so on and so forth. We can see the training levels pertinent to each of these categories. We see that in some cases we have high level, higher level or mid-level. These are the categories. The lowest training or education level is something that only has a low percentage here. Can you therefore confirm that the specialist training and education levels of special police members was exceptionally high, especially as compared to some other sectors within the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am able to confirm that. Within the special police itself, there was a situation. Everyone was encouraged to obtain university degrees and to join schools and get more education because this was needed for some of the posts, for people to apply to some posts. For example, if someone had a lower level of education, that person would be sent back to school, as it were. People were encouraged to go to university and allowances were made for people to be able to go back to studying and this was something that was wholeheartedly encouraged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please go to page 958 of the same document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is another table that we're looking at. These are disciplinary proceedings conducted against special police members throughout 1995. This table was produced in the same way as the previous one. The breakdown is based on the geographical police administrations and there is an special section here about the Lucko ATJ. If we look at the very last column or box, that's what I'm talking about, manning levels at the moment, 2311 employees, and then the percentage is given, as well as the number of disciplinary proceedings that were in progress, those to do with misdemeanours as well as those to do with more serious forms of crime, their total over 1995, 347 disciplinary proceedings against active duty members of the special police and that is the left-hand side of the table that we're looking at. The right-hand side of the table is about the reserve, 2444 members -- 64 members in 1995, 349 disciplinary complaints were filed against members. Is this consistent with your understanding of the situation back in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is completely consistent with what I knew the situation to be at the time. There were a number of disciplinary procedures that were in progress. This was a way to maintain and enforce discipline. The disciplinary Court, there was just one for all of the Ministry of Interior. It wasn't just for the special police. It applied to all other police formations as well and the court was independent in its work and it remains independent. For example, you couldn't have someone in the special police who was in a position to affect any action taken by this disciplinary court. It was up to them to start proceedings or to propose measures and then the court would take over and see the actual procedure through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the special police department did not have its own disciplinary court, right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't. There was just one for people from the ministry. That was at our HQ. There were various police administrations, for example the Osljak police administration had their own disciplinary court that was part of the Osljak police administration. The Zagreb court had no power over special police officers from Osljak. They had to be dealt with by the Osljak court that was part the Osijek police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All right. This is an disciplinary procedure and this has to do with disciplinary infractions or violations of the rules that pertain to discipline. Can you please explain more about this procedure. What if a member of the special police was found to have committed a crime. This is a more serious form the responsibility, this is not just a disciplinary infraction or violation. What happens then?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still an active duty police officer and this is the sort of problem that I encounter in my work on a daily basis and the same applied back in 1995 and the same procedure applied. I don't think anything has changed since in terms of procedure. If a member of the special police commits a crime all the general regulations and rules apply to him as to any other citizen. If the crime committed in the line of duty, then this prosecution is also conducted in the line of duty. There is an internal investigation. The member is as a rule suspended pending completion of the proceedings. There is normally a disciplinary procedure that is set in motion. At the same time, however, the investigators start an investigation and then an indictment is issued as soon as there are series of indicia of a crime. This person is investigated and tried just as any other citizen of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you said an investigation is conducted, are you referring to court investigation done by regular courts?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was done by regular courts but with the assistance of the crime investigation police. It's not that every court is involved in the whole investigation process. Some parts of the processes are done by the investigating police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After such police -- court investigation there are two options, either to suspend the investigation for the lack of evidence or -- due to other reasons, or the public prosecutor will issue an indictment against certain individuals. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After issuing an indictment comes a trial before the criminal court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. If a person is convicted of a crime he is automatically suspended from civil service; but if he is acquitted by the court and if, at that moment, the disciplinary proceedings have been completed and if the decision from the proceedings was that he would be removed from employment, then he is entitled to instigate administrative procedure to be reinstated in his job. If the suspension from job is not part of the conviction then he would be punished by some more lenient sanctions that do not affect his employment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like this document to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document number 65 ter 02452.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There 's no objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit number D528, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D528 is admitted into evidence. Could I ask one question, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We now have a rather detailed view on disciplinary actions taken against the members of the special police. Do you have any impression as to what the numbers are in relation to police investigations which resulted in indictments brought against the members of the special police units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please look at document 65 ter 05000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We can see that this document was drawn up by the special police sector on the 11th of January, 1996. It is addressed to Mr. Markac. And it is actually an annual report on the internal control sector work in 1995. This document mentions that the internal control sector, during 1995, was engaged in actually four segments. So they were involved in intelligence in operational preparations for operations in which special police took part. From your own experience and knowledge, can you tell us in what way, when you went to take part in certain operations, were prepared for that particular preparation? And by that I mean did you -- were you given information about what you can expect on the field, perhaps the number of the enemy troops that you might expect to face, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before any operation, we had briefings in which we agreed the tactics and how to operate within our area of responsibility. During these briefing sessions or preparatory meetings, I don't remember how we called them exactly but it had a name, when we discussed tactics, always one part of the meeting was dedicated to a presentation by someone from the internal control. He would inform us about the overall intelligence situation and prepare all the commanders in terms of passing on intelligence information about the enemy, their deployment, number of troops, positions, equipment, and all other relevant data that were available. Then they would give us this information. They were also in charge of preparing maps, in which this data were entered so that once we set off, we would have the enemy deployment already in the map. Yes, I can confirm this annual report in that it says that is it exactly what they did and that their role, in all operations, was what is in the army done by the army intelligence service. Essentially this is what they did for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Can you clarify to us item number 2, where it says that the internal control department took care of security and protection of the special police units.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that members of this section or department assessed the risks of the facilities in which the unit was billeted. They gathered intelligence information in order to assess the level of safety and security of our positions, where special police members were deployed. This would be briefly the explanation of this particular item.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Item 3: Professional training of members of the internal control and commanders of reconnaissance units. Can you shed some more light on this? What kind of activity this involved?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All reconnaissance units gathering information and the processing of intelligence was not only reserved from other intelligence services within the Croatian military, the secret service and the rest of it. Also, in each special unit we had our own reconnaissance and intelligence unit which was in charge of gathering directly on the ground information and intelligence about the enemy. And the internal control was in -- operationally in charge of running these units and using this data along with other data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Under item 4 it says that internal control was continuously monitoring interpersonal relations, relations between superiors and within the command structure. And if they would pinpoint any problems they would highlight them. Here there is mention of work discipline and a while ago you told us that the internal control did not conduct any disciplinary proceedings so how are we to understand then this particular task?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The internal control, in their job description and in practice, what I personally saw on a daily basis, monitored statistical data about breaches of discipline. They were given fortnightly reports from unit commanders and in the part which relates to disciplinary measures and proceedings, they would process these fortnightly or other reports and compile statistical data and analysis to be used by the head of the sector, by me or unit commanders. If in the course of their work the internal control were -- were to learn that someone had breached discipline and the commander failed to undertake any measures, although he knew about it, then through the head of the section, this department will warn the commander that one of his men had breached discipline, but that would also be up to me to do that. If I had had this knowledge it would only be natural for me to inform that somebody had done something and that this person should be punished for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. If we move now to page 715 of this document, and that's two pages forward. Item 4, in the upper part of the page. Yes, that's right. Here we see that the internal control continuously monitored the work of special police and the system of information distribution. Therefore, they had constant insight into the situation in units in order to undertake preventative actions. The department highlighted the floors in the work, the relations between officers, disciplinary problems. They monitored how the structure was developing and dealt with other services in terms of observing how tasks are being carried out. Mr. Janic, can you give us any comment on this part of the report on the work of the internal control? Is it consistent with what you remember and know?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is exactly what this department did, among other things. If, in the course of their work, they received information about someone committing something, they would send this information through their own channels to the unit commander instructing him to undertake certain disciplinary procedure, and I think that is the same to what I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have this document admitted into evidence and that's 65 ter 05000.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number D529.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D529 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the recently admitted document, P587, please. That's 65 ter 03342. This is in case it doesn't have designation P.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A short while ago, Mr. Janic, you had an opportunity to see this order dated 15 November 1995, addressed to the heads of police administrations, to the head of the special police sector, to the commander of the Lucko anti-terrorist unit and to the commander of the air force unit. So this order was issued by Mr. Markac, and it refers to the issue of discipline that you so extensively spoke about. Can you confirm that this order reflects also what you said, that commanders of units were authorised to impose discipline?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were independent in their work, and they were responsible for imposing discipline and if there was a breach of discipline, they were responsible for instituting disciplinary procedure. This is what they were authorised for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in another aspect of this document. It was issued by the special police sector. However, if we look into the introductory part of this which says: "Upon completion of an analysis of the work and discipline with the organisational units of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Croatia conducted at the advisory board of the minister, Mr. Ivan Jarnjak, and in view of a need to eliminate the irregularities observed in operation, conduct of the members of active and reserve units of the special police, I hereby issue the following order." Mr. Janic, can you confirm that this order was sent both to the special police but also to other sectors of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. This was dealt with at --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. There is no indication here that it has gone to any other units. It is to the special police units from -- on the basis of this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It reads all police administration chiefs which -- and then to be handed over to specialised police units, so therefore at least was not directly addressed to the special police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Or exclusively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or -- yes, it doesn't say that -- with whom it had to be shared apart from these specialised police units. But it seems to be a minor issue. Mr. Misetic, do you have a major issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't think it is major but it is something I just wanted to alert the Trial Chamber to, during the break we're having communications with the Prosecution about the translation of one word in that paragraph. That relates to in the original the translation of the phrase [B/C/S spoken], which has been translated here as "in operation" which is a translation that we believe leads to confusion. We believe that the proper translation should be "in the work and conduct," and that actually was a subject of come confusion between the Prosecution and the Defence and we'll probably seek a clarification of the translation. Just so that the record is complete, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the parties together could find the resources which finally will lead to the ultimate translation of this phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. Janic, continue with what you were explaining. You said that this order actually was generated at the meeting of the collegium of ministers.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decisions taken at the collegium refer to all the sectors of the ministry. At the time, in 1995, there were three sectors. That was regular police, that was crime police, and that was special police and these orders inadvertently --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- invariably referred to all three segments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does this conclusion of yours stem from how this letter was addressed? It says all police administrations.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The head was -- the head was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter kindly asks the witness to repeat his last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- could you please repeat your last answer, which was not caught by the interpreters. You said "the head was ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. I said that the chief of the police administration was also the head of his special unit but also to all other police units within his administration including the crime police and the regular police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's see how discipline worked in practice. Next up is a 65 ter document 05225. This is a document dated October 1995. It was issued by Mr. Markac, and it was sent to the head of the Zadar and Knin police administration. It says that it must be submitted to the special police unit commander, the unit attached to that police administration, the purpose of this document being verification of certain data. It say that an Official Note reached the police administration from the Gracac police branch and the note states that on the 17th of September, 1995 four special police members were observed driving in a vehicle with certain licence plates and they were spotted moving away from a family home that was set fire to, as well as the shed next to it with haystacks in it. The registration plates are known to the Zadar-Knin police administration and that is why a check is requested. Based on your recollection, was this one of the ways in which, in practical terms, issues regarding discipline were dealt with within the special police sector?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The general applied rigorous standards in this respect. It is quite obvious that the special police unit commander did not have this note from the Gracac police station. This is how the system worked. The information first got to the special police sector and then the special police sector forwards this in such a way to the commander of that special police unit and then he further processed this, given his power to first establish the facts and then if the facts show that someone did something or other, what follows next is disciplinary steps that are taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have a number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President, just for the record again this is one of the documents that was tendered in the bar table submission last night. For the record, it is document number 12 on the list, Mr. President, so that there won't be any confusion at the end of these proceedings if there is time I will indicate what documents have been tendered into evidence today from that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you then remove that from the list or mark them on the list in such a way that Mr. Registrar does not assign duplicate numbers to the same document. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number D530.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D530 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have 65 ter document 05227.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is a report produced by the Zadar and Knin police administration, the special police unit specifically. The date is 4 October 1995, addressed to the special police sector. The person issuing the document is the special police unit commander, Mr. Vrsalje [phoen]. The report talks about the fact that the report itself is a result of the request that we looked at a while ago, the request made by the special police sector, specifically Mr. Markac, and it says that the check was conducted and that it was established beyond reasonable doubt that the arsonists in the village of Potkorina, unknown house number, was a man named Ivan Kovac, a member of the special police unit of the Zadar and Knin police administration. The document goes on to describe what exactly was established. It was established that he was together with another three members of the special police. They drove over to that village where he set fire to this building. The other three members were not involved and he was the only one who was now facing disciplinary measures. He was dismissed from his post as special police group leader. And 10 percent of his next salary was deducted. There was a mitigating circumstance relating to the perpetrator. He had a clear police record and his performance had, up to that point, been impeccable. Mr. Janic, isn't this exactly along the same lines with what you were telling us the special police unit members were authorised to impose discipline in these units?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what this confirms. They initiated their own disciplinary procedures. There were certain kinds of procedures where they had the power to take decisions and impose punishment but that was in relation to certain types of infractions and sometimes they would initiate proceedings and then a court would take over and potentially prosecute or try the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This, in a way, anticipate my next question. We're looking here at a crime, an offence, which at least at first sight bears the hallmarks of a crime because there is property destroyed and the safety of persons is potentially jeopardised. I'm not sure if you know about the specific case, but was it possible to have a disciplinary procedure and a criminal complaint filed with the state prosecutor in parallel and then there is an independent procedure, criminal procedure that is underway which does not in any way depend on the disciplinary procedure that is in progress?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, the two are not necessarily related. In this case I'm not sure what the police did or did not do, but they could have investigated this and they could have filed a criminal complaint. And this had nothing to do with the commander's decision to filing a complaint and this had nothing to do with a potential disciplinary procedure. The two procedures are not necessarily related. They become related if there is a criminal complaint and there has not yet been a disciplinary procedure so if a criminal complaint is filed and then the disciplinary complaint was not filed, then once a criminal procedure is started, you must have a disciplinary complaint to be able to launch a criminal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have a number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President in fact, this is also another document that was submitted. It looks like Mr. Mikulicic and I are both on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You seem to have a shared, a common interest in certain matters. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number D531.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. D531 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one question to clarify. Mr. Janic, you -- you said several times a criminal complaint could have been filed. What was the determining factor on whether -- where apparently a crime had been committed, whether or not a criminal complaint is filed? This is complaint by the victim or is it a complaint by the police officers investigating the matter? Could you tell us what would trigger the filing of a criminal complaint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to explain. The document came from the Gracac police station. It has its own head. They have their own crime police units, civilian police and so on and so forth. They were entirely autonomous, independent, and it was up to them to judge the gravity of a crime and perhaps file a criminal report. Based on their assessment of the crime itself, they sent a note to the special police sector, but this has nothing to do with the fact that they may or may not have decided to go ahead with this. If they had any evidence, if they were any indicia of a crime being committed, they could have filed a criminal report to the appropriate court within their own area. This is what would have triggered criminal proceedings. And this was down to the Gracac police station. What steps they took in this particular case is not something that I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Can we please have 3D00-1467.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As we're waiting for the document to come up, let me ask you this. Earlier on we talked about the fact that within the special police sector there was training, specialised training, courses and so on and so forth. This is a document that dates back to the beginning of 1995. It is addressed to Mr. Markac. The document contains information about the types of teaching and courses that were organised. If you look at page 14, among other things of this document, you see Roman numeral XI, theory and specialised subject matter, a total of 20 teaching hours. It says that issues to do with international law of war were studied. This is something that you have already confirmed. Can you now again confirm that this was the case in the special police sector also on the eve of Operation Storm, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm in a position to confirm that. Each time there was a seminar or a course that was organised and held, unless it was a specialist course for divers or some such, but the one I'm looking at right now, this was a seminar for special police leaders. This was part of the teaching programme, international law of war, that was one of the topics tackled. This was something that we studied at the time since we were at war but even before then we knew that Croatia was occupied to a large extent, Croatia's territory, there would be other operations, we knew that, it was only logical that we should get our people to understand more and familiarize themselves with the rules and provisions of international law of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we move on to page 15, that's the next page, you said Croatia was at war and more operations were expected. Page 15 Roman numeral XII, chapter 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I look at the whole of the document as it was uploaded in e-court and I find in English a three-page document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What we are about to see on the screen, Mr. Janic, is the minutes of the meeting between the president of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Franjo Tudjman, and a delegation of the military, held on the 17th July 1995 on Brioni. General Markac was also present at this meeting, and here I would like to refer you to page 48 of this record. This is ERN page 01324928. Of course, we are not going to analyse the entire record of this meeting, but we shall rather focus on the subject that is of interest to us at this point, and that is the duties and the tasks and the work of special police. At the meeting, Mr. Markac took to the floor, and, in his address, Mr. Markac warned and I -- oh, I apologise, I gave you a wrong page. And we'll go back to this one later. But now I'd like to see page 1329 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is the page 27 of the transcript, and the ERN number is 01324961. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Mr. Markac took to the floor here and addressed the president of the republic about the use and the purpose of special purpose units. And he said that there should be a tactical reserve of rapid action special forces which, based on good assessment and good use by the staff, and you can find this on the next page, page 28, can you be used in any part of the territory of the Republic of Croatia. These forces, continues Mr. Markac, have been involved in a number of major military operations and have demonstrated that they were prepared and mobile and most importantly capable within very short period of time, six to eight hours, to have all their forces ready and deployed in the expected areas. At the end of his address, which is on page 30, ERN number 01324964, Mr. Markac concluded by saying: "Mr. President," this is to President Tudjman, "I estimate that we are ready to carry out any task but I would like to draw your attention to the fact that we have to be given a specific task." Mr. Janic, according to your understanding and knowledge can you explain to us how you in the special police interpreted this specific or this special purpose task?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special purpose task would mean that there are some specific features in terms of the capabilities of special police which is an outcome of a long-term training, education, and experience acquired in the previous operations. The special police had the status of a firm and elite unit, capable of carrying out the most difficult tasks under the most difficult circumstances. For instance, in mountains, in forbidden terrain, in winter time. That is to say, in the conditions in which other military units were not able to move around large forces. Under such circumstances, through their training and through their way of work, the special police had demonstrated and here they say that they are ready to take on such special purpose tasks in future as well. And this is exactly what happened later in the Storm. So by operating in difficult conditions, in mountainous areas, et cetera, these operations could have only be done by elite units, special units like ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we now move to page 48 of this record; this is ERN number 01324982, this is part of President Tudjman's speech, and we see that this is what he says here by referring to the address of General Markac: "General Markac has mentioned the problem of special forces of the internal affairs. When there were no other legal or constitutional possibilities, as you know, we have started forming the Croatian army from among the ranks of the ministry and this particularly refers to special internal affairs forces who played a pivotal role in all the operations that we had so far. However, we also have to be realistic about this. We do not need to make a special or separate parallel army out of these special units. Therefore they should maintain the features that they have had, since the liberation until the war in Croatia and Bosnia is over, and then we shall decide finally what to do. Until then, they should remain as they are, and the task given to them would be such that would be part of joint operations that can be carried out and they can easily be carried out or even better by them than by some other units." Mr. Janic, would you agree with me from these quotations it turns out that at the very top government level, and I'm referring to President Tudjman and the ministers present there, in a certain way it has been established how special police should look like and how it should work within the ministry as unit dedicated to special tasks.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one can say that. The state leadership with President Tudjman at its helm had information about the special police. They recognise the achievements we made during the war and they appreciate our contribution to the war of independence. Their assessment was that, since full liberation of Croatia was being planned, this demonstrates that within these operations, particularly in view of the skill and expertise of the special police, they were counted upon as a very serious unit intended for special purpose tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have now 65 ter document number 04484.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Before we discuss this document, Mr. Janic, let us move to another subject. On the eve of Operation Storm, I would like to discuss the situation in Velebit with respect to special police units. Can you please tell us, in a few sentences, and bearing in mind the time that we have available, what the task of special police were -- was in Velebit, not only at that time but also two or three years before?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be brief. You know that the occupied territories were very close to the shoreline. There was only one road connecting northern parts of Croatia with its southern part and that was the highway and it ran next to the Mount Velebit. There was absolutely a need to prospect this road from the attacks by Serbs across Mount Velebit. They were capable of attacking it. In view of the specific features of these mountains and very hard conditions of operating in a mountainous area, this task was assigned to special police. In 1992 it covered the area from Gospic to southern slope of Velebit. Our task was to defend the only road connecting the northern and southern Croatia from a possible -- from a possibility of its being cut off. From 1992, positions were taken up on Velebit. The code-name was Poskok 1, later it was renamed Poskok 2. The special police held the defence line from northern to southern Velebit and this line with some changes following the Maslenica operation, remained the same after Operation Storm. And that was the point of departure for special police in Operation Storm. So this is what we did on Mount Velebit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the special police was based immediately before Operation Storm and throughout that period? I'm referring to the command headquarters.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command headquarters of special police on Mount Velebit was as follows. The main logistical base was in a place --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get name of place.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- directly on the sea shore. I think in the place called Libinje on Velebit was a forward command post which commanded the special police forces on Velebit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you describe this geographical area? Is this a populated area? Can you just illustrate what we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Velebit is the highest mountain in Croatia. It is very harsh. The conditions for life are very difficult there. There is no human population there. It is particularly difficult in winter time because winters are long. There is lots of snow and the weather is -- conditions are difficult. Staying on Velebit throughout these years, the special police gained invaluable experience in operating in difficult mountainous areas as well as in the defending or holding a defence line. So this experience of two or three years of defending Velebit was the basis in tactical terms for later successes achieved in Operation Storm which ensued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did you solve logistical problems, food supplies, weapons, materiel and everything else that is required for having a unit operating and functioning normally?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had our own logistical service and base on Mount Velebit and the entire MUP logistical service relied on it, starting from equipment, procurement department, financial and materiel procurement department. We had their assistance in that domain. Supplies were initially provided in a way by using horses as the most simple and most practical means of transportation along mountainous paths. We had logistical teams providing and transferring food and equipment. However, under harsh weather conditions we could only use horses or pack animals for providing supplies to the units on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you properly, the special police units, in Velebit, spent quite a long time before Operation Storm. How long?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you meaning -- are you referring to the combat deployment or preparations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Preparations.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During July, as far as I know, and I was personally there, we thought that this was going to be real action which later became Storm. It was around -- on or around 29th of July. We were on Velebit and within our area of responsibility we were given the objectives of the operation, which were similar or identical to those of Operation Storm. After two or three days on Mount Velebit this operation was recalled. I don't know whether this was treated as an exercise or whatever, but one could say that that was a dress rehearsal for Operation Storm. After that, we had a detailed analysis of this so-called action that was aborted because at that time, there were more than 2.000 men in position on Velebit, including artillery and equipment, as if it were a real operation, and we learned some lessons and drew some conclusions with regard to communications and tactical terms and this was applicable and applied later in the actual Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to next page of the document on the screen. Let me draw your attention to the fact that the title of this document is handwritten and it says that this is an order issued to General Mladen Markac for Operation Storm. This is a document dated 26th June 1995 and I assume, and correct me if I'm wrong, that this is it precisely what you just told us about a minute ago. This is a document issued by the Main Staff of the Croatian army. At the time the chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian army was General Janko Bobetko and it was submitted to the commander of the special units of the MUP, Colonel General Mladen Markac. So, according to this document an order is being given to the special forces of the Ministry of Interior to -- from the operational base in Velebit and what follows are the names and locations which later we're going to see in the map. An order is given to launch attacks along certain axis in order to capture Mali Golic, Sveti Rok, Gracac and Prezid. It is specifically said that they need to cut off the road leading from Gospic to Gracac, in the section between Sveti Rok and Stikada, that they need to capture a radio relay transmitter at Celavac, that they need to place under their supervision the pass at Prezid and to link up with the forces of the military district of Split and place under surveillance and supervision road Jasanica, [unintelligible], Prezid and Vusic [phoen]. The next page of this order, could you please turn the page chief Bobetko issues the following order. The operation is to be carried out in two stages over a total of three days. Then there is a detailed description of what stage 1 and stage 2 respectively would comprise. If you look at item 3, it says that all the remaining forces should perform active defence. If there is a favourable tactical situation that arises, there should be attacks as well in order to pose a threat to the Medak-Sveti Rok road. It also says there should be coordination the district area -- recruitment area commander in Split the people in Zagreb and the command of the 27th Guards Brigade. The special police forces must be ready by the 29th of June at 5.00. The order is forwarded also to the commanders of the Split and Gospic recruitment areas. This is order that brought you and another 2.000 special police members to Velebit early in June. An operation was expected, which never got off the ground. You were then withdrawn from Velebit, right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I do apologise. I was wrong by about a month a while ago as I was speaking. I was talking about July and it was actually June. I would like to correct that. Yes, this was the order for that particular operation which was never carried out. We were convinced that we would be launching this operation. We were perfectly ready on the day and by the hour and we had prepared well for all these tasks specified here. We were fully ready to perform this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I suppose you have noticed this, too and I think everybody else in this courtroom has noticed, there is no explicit mention of the word Storm or Operation Storm in this order is there?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is none.

utterances.text: D535 is admitted into evidence. Could I put one question to you, Mr. Janic. What we see here is that staff general Janko Bobetko is giving orders, he is an army authority, he is giving orders to Mr. Markac who is in the Ministry of Interior. Not a request. It is an order with quite some operational details; what to do, when to do it, and what order to do it. Could you explain how a military commander would give orders to a police commander how to deploy his forces and what they should do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. The special police at the time was part of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia. It was now back to it performing military operations. All orders for military operations were issued to everyone by the Chief of Staff, head of the Main Staff of the Croatian army. I'm sure the minister would approve that sort of thing previously. I don't quite remember, but all war operations were run from a war centre, from a military centre. Each of the orders was given by a commander and that applies to this one as well. We were but a component of our armed forces. We were police, but at this point in time we were also part of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following this decision by General Bobetko concerning the withdrawal of forces from Velebit you withdrew. What happened now. We are now in early July 1995.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the units went back to their own police administration areas except for those who were still watching the defence lines along Velebit. Then there was some preparations that were carried out. It was clear that an operation was imminent. There was some tactical preparations. There were parts of Velebit that were reconnoitred by the reconnaissance operative groups. They carried out reconnaissance in the area, they gathered intelligence on the enemy forces that there were and their positions. We scouted the enemy lines. We gathered intelligence, we drew up anlayses, and the operation was in the pipeline. It was being planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You say the operation involved the presence of over 2.000 special unit members on Velebit. How did this group coming together? How was it put together?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We called them collective forces or special purpose forces. That would be military jargon for that, the kind they use today. They would stay in their own police administration areas going about their daily tasks but whenever it was necessary, and this was one such situation, there would be an assessment as to how many men would be needed to perform a certain operation and then the special police sector in a situation like this based on such an assessment would call up a number of units, a number of men, 3.000 if that's what they thought they needed, then 3.000 would be called up, you know, 15 units each comprising 150 or 200 people. At this point in time we had these groups that were put together under a single command and there was only one purpose to their work. They would carry out a couple of tasks that were provisional tasks, and as soon as these tasks were completed, the special purpose forces or groups would be dissolved and each of the original units would say go back to their own respective police administration areas and they would go back to their daily work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All right. Just to make sure that my understanding is correct. There were a total of 19 police administrations there, part of which were also the special police units and the Lucko ATJ. A certain number of men were called up who then set up this group, collective force group, if I may call it that, and this went on operating as an independent group and it had a particular mission or objective, right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All right. So once a group like that was formed, under whose command within the special police sector were they or was it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were under the operative command of the chief of the special police sector. Of course if you look at the chain of command there is also General Markac [Realtime transcript read in error "Cermak"], the number one man of the special police units. But in an operative sense in terms of control, this was something for the chief of the special police sector. He was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Therefore, not all special police unit members were part of this collective group, as it were. Some of them remained with their original police administrations, didn't they? Under whose command were those police members?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As long as they stayed back within their own police administrations, they would be under the command of their own chief, the chief of their police administration. Not everyone was called up to be part of these collective groups as it were, because we were still holding positions at the time down in Croatian south around Prevlaka, the Prevlaka isthmus, and we had some forces in Western Slavonia after Operation Flash. Therefore, it wasn't possible to physically assemble all of them.

Thank you. I will then now deliver the Chamber's decision on the Prosecution's motion for evidence to be presented via video-conference link and submission of Rule 92 ter statements and associated exhibits for witness 53. The Chamber defers the part of the part of the motion dealing with the submission of witness statements and one exhibit pursuant to Rule 92 ter to the time when the witness will testify. This decision deals merely with the part of the motion to hear witness 53 via video-conference link. The proposed date of testimony is the 17th of July, 2008. The Defence for the three accused responded on the 9th and 10th July that they do not oppose the part of the motion requesting testimony via video-conference link. According to Rule 81 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, a Chamber may order that proceedings be conducted by way of video-conference link if this is consistent with the interests of justice. As previously set out by this Chamber, the standard of Rule 81 bis is met if a witness is unable to come to the Tribunal, if the testimony is sufficiently important to make it unfair to the requesting party to proceed without it, and if the accused is not prejudiced in his or her right to confront the witness. The Prosecution submits that the witness is unable to come to The Hague to testify due to a back disorder. According to a medical certificate attached to the Prosecution's motion, the disorder makes Witness 53 unfit to travel. The Chamber is satisfied that the witness is unable to come to the Tribunal. Having reviewed the two witness statements made by the witness in 2003 and 2007, the Chamber accepts that the testimony is sufficiently important to make it unfair to the Prosecution to proceed without it. Finally, the Defence has not argued and the Chamber does not find that the accused will be prejudiced in the exercise of their right to confront the witness if testimony via video-conference link is granted. For the foregoing reasons, the Chamber finds that it is consistent with the interests of justice to hear the testimony of witness 53 via video-conference link and grants the motion. The Chamber requests the registrar to make the necessary arrangements for a video-conference link for the testimony on or about the 17th of July, 2008. And this conclude the Chamber's decision. As far as Witness 172 is concerned, I have not yet -- the Chamber has not yet prepared a decision in such detail as I just read for witness 53. However, because we first wanted to look at the Gotovina Defence objections against hearing witness 172's testimony through video link, the Chamber has meanwhile considered it and the Chamber came to the conclusion that it will granted motion in respect of video link testimony for witness 172 as well. And I put this now on the record mainly to facilitate the preparations for the Registrar. A similar -- a decision like I just read for Witness 53 will be read for Witness 172 once we have prepared it. We stand adjourned until tomorrow.
